ingest.title: BBH File Ingestion Framework Design Document
ingest.author: SEI Professional Services
ingest.scope: Landing-zone discovery through Oracle RAW load, end-of-run completeness and SLA evaluation, the DATE_CONTROL transition, the downstream trigger, recovery and monitoring.
ingest.hands_over: Triggers the separate Transformation DAG once the expected file set is complete. STG through Gold is not its concern.

dbt.title: BBH dbt Transformation Design Document
dbt.author: SEI Professional Services
dbt.scope: Transformation from SWP_RAW through approved Gold: the STG source-DQ view, the INT PASS filter, DIM-before-FACT sequencing and MERGE against the pre-existing Gold tables, plus DQ capture, reconciliation and publishing to Splunk.
dbt.hands_over: Advances TRIGGER to COMPLETE and seeds the next PENDING business date on success. File generation, transfer, discovery, header and trailer validation and the RAW load are outside it.

SEI_BOUNDARY.line: the guarded PENDING → TRIGGER update on DATE_CONTROL
SEI_BOUNDARY.note: The Ingestion DAG owns PENDING → TRIGGER. Only the run whose UPDATE changes exactly one row may invoke transformation — that is how two scheduled runs five minutes apart cannot both trigger it. The Transformation DAG owns TRIGGER → COMPLETE and the creation of the next PENDING row, in one database transaction, and it re-checks completeness defensively before doing any work.
ev: File Ingestion design doc Appendix E.3 (p.24)

SEI_COMPONENTS.w: The files SEI produces for BBH, delivered to an SFTP location.

Copies COMPLETE SWP files from SFTP into the Landing Zone. The word complete is carrying weight: the design assumes a file only appears once it is whole, and if that is not true a readiness convention such as a final rename or a marker file has to be added.
Shared storage that Airflow scans for eligible files. Shared is load-bearing too — every worker pod has to see the same Landing, Archive and Quarantine folders.
Where a file goes after processing. Archive on success, Quarantine when validation fails before anything is written.
ONE DAG for every inbound interface, not one per interface. It is driven by configuration rows, so a new interface is onboarded by adding a row rather than by writing a DAG.

A scan on a schedule rather than a sensor waiting on each file. It reads the active configurations, scans the Landing Zone, matches each physical filename to exactly one logical interface and parses the business date out of the filename.
Airflow creates one task per discovered file at run time, so files process independently and in parallel within the pool and Oracle connection limits. A file never waits for another interface.

Per file: claim the (interface, business date) pair in the registry, validate readability, header, trailer, zero-row policy and row counts, load the detail rows into the configured RAW table in ONE Oracle transaction, reconcile parsed against trailer against inserted counts, and commit only when they agree. Then move the file and record the outcome.

The last task of EVERY ingestion run, including runs that found no files at all — which is the point, because yesterday's late file can complete the set without a new one arriving today. It compares the expected active daily interfaces against the interfaces already ARCHIVED for the open business date.

A single UPDATE with STATUS='PENDING' in the WHERE clause. If it changes one row, this run owns the trigger and invokes transformation with the deterministic run id transform__<BUSINESS_DATE>. If it changes zero rows, another run already did, and this one stops.

For the gap between acquiring TRIGGER and the transformation run actually existing. A scheduled check retries when the row says TRIGGER, the transformation run id is null and no matching deterministic run can be found.

Missing files at or after the cutoff: keep PENDING, do not trigger, publish a correlated breach alert. Correlation is event type plus business date, so a breach raises one alert rather than one per five-minute cycle. When the date later completes, publish recovery and then trigger.
Re-checks completeness and TRIGGER status before doing any work — trust but verify — then builds the layers in order, each as a build task followed by its own test task.
Standardises the source columns and computes a pass or fail verdict per row. Stores nothing: it is recomputed on read.
Reads only the rows that passed, maps the code sets, keyed on the natural business key plus business date, partitioned, purged by partition drop after seven days.
History by direct-compare MERGE into tables that already exist. The surrogate key comes from the Oracle sequence already in use. No DDL is issued against Gold.
Loads only transactions whose dimension has resolved. A transaction whose account has not arrived is never written with a placeholder key — it is held and replayed once the dimension exists.
Every failing record is written to one store and held at the layer that caught it. A step after the fact build picks up the rows that can now resolve, loads them and marks them resolved.
Counts at four boundaries for the business date, written to an immutable log and published. The pass or warning verdict is derived on the Splunk side, after the data is already in Gold.

The final task. Advances the date and inserts the next PENDING row with its resolved cutoff, in one transaction, only on full success. On failure the date stays TRIGGER and no next date is created, so the pipeline is locked rather than drifting.
Owns all dashboards, counts, trending and alerting, for both documents. Oracle keeps the durable logs; Splunk reports from the events published to it and does the alert correlation.

3.why: The real-time API lane. Both documents are batch, end to end.

4.why: The loader endpoints BBH submits to. Outbound, and neither document covers outbound at all.

5.why: How SEI produces the files. The ingestion document puts file generation outside itself in as many words.

6.why: SEI's own orchestration. Out of scope for both.

7.why: SEI's monitoring surface. Out of scope for both.

9.why: SEI does not use arrival sensors. It runs a scheduled scan every five minutes and decides completeness at the END of the run, as a set difference. A sensor per interface is the pattern it was written to avoid.

10.why: Outbound to SEI. Neither document has an outbound path.

11.why: The API lane. Both SEI documents are batch from end to end — files in, Gold out — and neither mentions a proxy, a gateway or a synchronous call.

12.why: The API lane, as above. Nothing in either document describes real-time access to this data.

15.why: One tracker component, two SEI objects: STG is a view that stores nothing, INT is a table kept seven days.

16.why: One tracker component, two ordered SEI layers — and the tables already exist, so dbt populates rather than builds them.

17.why: SEI gives it the rule it was missing: a closed interval is corrected by direct UPDATE, never by MERGE.

18.why: SEI has two DAGs, not one, and no per-domain fan-out: parallelism comes from one mapped task per FILE, created at run time.

20.why: Directly contradicted rather than merely absent: SEI permits one non-COMPLETE business date at a time, enforced by a unique index. An intraday cadence does not fit that state machine.

21.why: SEI's replay is not an engine. It is one task at the end of the transformation run, driven by the open rows in the DQ store and bounded by INT's seven days.

22.why: SEI has no partial-set path: the transition fires only on an empty missing set. Running on what arrived would be a design change.

23.why: The ingestion document specifies exactly this: readable, header, trailer, zero-row and the date, all before any RAW write, and a failure goes to QUARANTINED.

24.why: Nothing profiles RAW. The first thing that reads a row's content in SEI's design is the STG view, already past the load.

26.why: SEI reconciles, but not as a gate. The counts are computed and published AFTER the fact build and the verdict is derived in Splunk, so a mismatch alerts rather than blocks.

29.why: Two different quarantines. SEI quarantines FILES before load, and for failed ROWS keeps lineage only — no payload copy — on the assumption that anything held resolves inside seven days.

31.why: Business date, run ids, the source record id and the failure category are correlated; the control tables are the ledger.

32.why: Credentials in OpenShift secrets, and the loader account holds only the DML it needs — no ALTER, DROP or CREATE.

35.why: This catalogue. SEI gives all reporting to Splunk, so 360 reading the same tables directly is BBH's addition — defensible, and nobody has written down who owns which.

36.why: Sign-on for BBH's own tools. Out of scope for both.

37.why: Downstream of Gold. Both documents stop at Gold.

38.why: Downstream of Gold. Both documents stop once DIM and FACT are written, so how IMDS is fed is BBH's to design.

39.why: Downstream of Gold, as above — and SEI's design has no notion of a consumer-specific shape at all.

40.why: Not built this phase, and not in either document.

41.why: Reporting off the warehouse. Outside both documents, which end at the Gold tables.

42.why: The real-time lane again. Neither document has a consumer that is not fed from a completed business date.

43.why: The existing BBH estate. Both documents describe what arrives and what is built, never who consumes it.

44.why: Platform build. Neither document covers it.

45.why: Container images. Both documents assume OpenShift and neither specifies how images are built or versioned — only that rollback is redeploying the prior one.

46.why: Registry, scanning and signing. Not mentioned, and it is the supply-chain half of a design that is otherwise explicit about least privilege.

47.why: Named, and narrowly: least privilege, and DML only on the Gold tables.

48.why: Oracle, SFTP and storage credentials in OpenShift secrets, referenced through Airflow connections.

49.why: Network policy and egress. Neither document says what the pipeline is allowed to reach, which matters given it pulls from SFTP and pushes to Splunk.

50.why: SEI needs one specific thing from storage and states it as an assumption: Landing, Archive and Quarantine must be shared across worker pods, or mapped tasks cannot reliably read or move files.

51.why: A starting configuration is given: schedule every five minutes, catchup off, one active run, pool 8 to 10, one or two retries.

52.why: Worker pods are how file-level concurrency scales, bounded by pools and Oracle connections.

53.why: Resource quotas and priority. The documents give a starting pool size and worker count and leave the cluster-level envelope open — see open decision O2.

54.why: Warm start and pre-pulled images. A latency optimisation for a five-minute discovery cycle that neither document considers.

55.why: Pool size is sized against Oracle connection capacity, and the document says the number is a starting position to confirm.

56.why: Node placement. Not mentioned, though the shared-storage assumption for Landing, Archive and Quarantine constrains it.

57.why: Git-versioned models and DAGs; the pipeline compiles and runs unit and DQ tests before promotion.

58.why: GitOps and ArgoCD. The dbt document says models and DAGs are Git-versioned and promoted as tagged images; it does not name a deployment tool.

59.why: Rollback is redeploying the prior image, and it is safe only because Gold writes are idempotent merges with no DDL.

60.why: Nothing covers schema change management, which matters more here than usual: SEI's design forbids DDL against Gold, so whatever does change those tables sits outside it.

61.why: Blue-green and canary for the API lane, which neither document has.

62.why: Neither document covers availability or recovery of the platform itself.

63.why: Backup and restore is not in either document.

64.why: SEI gives every dashboard, trend and alert to Splunk. A separate monitoring stack is a second place for the same job.

65.why: Cost and capacity are not in either document.

BBH_LAYERS.note: Stage 2, Silver and Enriched are one layer under three names. Inside it: STG is a view, held in memory, and its job is the source DQ check. INT, DIM and FACT together are the normalised SWP data model, with reference mapping and translation applied.
BBH_LAYERS.beyond: Above that sit two layers SEI's documents do not describe: a PRE-GOLD layer shaped as a mirror of IMDS and PBDW, and then a simple movement of that data into the actual warehouse. SEI's design publishes straight from DIM and FACT and stops.
BBH_LAYERS.why_it_matters: It changes what Gold means. In SEI's documents DIM and FACT are the approved Gold tables and the end of the line. In BBH's model they are the normalised middle, and Gold is the consumer-shaped mirror above them. Both cannot be the published contract, and which one is decides where reconciliation has to end.
BBH_LAYERS.src: BBH, stated directly — not from either SEI document

BBH_EXTENSION.n: Pre-Gold · mirror of IMDS and PBDW
BBH_EXTENSION.w: Consumer-shaped tables that mirror the warehouses they feed, built from the normalised model below them.
BBH_EXTENSION.why: Neither SEI document has a layer above DIM and FACT. The dbt document treats DIM and FACT as the approved Gold tables and publishes from there.

BBH_EXTENSION.w: A simple data movement from the mirror into the actual warehouse — extract, transport, load, verify. No transformation in flight.
BBH_EXTENSION.why: SEI's design ends at DIM and FACT. Nothing in either document describes moving data onward, or what proves the movement arrived intact.

INT, DIM and FACT together, with reference mapping and translation applied. Passing rows only; INT keeps seven days; dimensions are built before facts so a transaction can always find its account.

The real-time lane. Neither SEI document mentions it — both are batch from end to end — so nothing here is cited.

Everything going back to SEI. A consumer such as CRM calls the Hub's API with the loader details and the data; the Hub validates it and transforms it into loader format; SEI PS processes the loader; the Hub calls the consumer's own API with the response. Two APIs, one each way, and neither SEI design document has an outbound path at all.

The path both SEI documents describe: a scheduled scan, one mapped task per file, validate, load RAW in one transaction, reconcile three counts, archive.
Looking at what landed before anything is done to it. Not in SEI's design — the first thing that reads a row's content there is the STG view.

orchestration.w: Owns the business date up to the handoff: evaluate completeness and the SLA, take the guarded transition, invoke transformation, and recover a trigger that never started.
Re-checks before it starts, builds the layers in order with a test task between each, and advances the date only on full success.
DATE_CONTROL: one row per business date, PENDING to TRIGGER to COMPLETE, at most one date open at a time.

processing.w: The stage chain itself — the view, the persisted middle and the two Gold layers, all as version-controlled SQL.
The row-level pass or fail, the store that holds what failed, the replay that clears it, and the counts across four boundaries.
Stage 3 and what reads it. SEI's documents end at DIM and FACT, so nothing in this lane is cited.

foundation.w: The small tables the run depends on: what is expected, what arrived, and which date is open.
Where the run proves what it did. SEI gives every dashboard and alert to Splunk; 360 reads the same tables directly.
What happens to a bad record, and how a number is traced back to the file it came from.
Credentials in secrets, and a loader account that can change rows in Gold but cannot create, alter or drop anything.

openshift.w: Namespaces, images, registry, RBAC, secrets, network policy and storage.
The Airflow deployment, worker pods, quotas, and the Oracle connection envelope the pool size is sized against.
Git-versioned models and DAGs, compiled and tested before promotion; rollback is redeploying the prior image.

SEI_ARCH_DOC.author: SEI

ARCH_CONFLICTS.arch: RAW_ACCOUNT, RAW_CLIENT, RAW_TAXLOT, RAW_TRANSACTION, RAW_POSITION, RAW_CORRECTED_TRANSACTION, RAW_CORRECTED_POSITION.
ARCH_CONFLICTS.doc: The dbt design document names three: account, client and transaction. Position, tax lot and the two correction tables do not appear in it at all.
ARCH_CONFLICTS.why: Four of the seven feeds have no transformation designed for them. If the architecture is right, the design document covers under half the inbound surface.

ARCH_CONFLICTS.t: Stage 2 as five tables, or as STG plus INT
ARCH_CONFLICTS.arch: Five STG2_* tables, materialised as tables, full refresh daily or incremental.
ARCH_CONFLICTS.doc: A STG view that stores nothing, plus an INT table kept seven days and partitioned.
ARCH_CONFLICTS.why: Not a naming difference. One stores Stage 2 and one does not, and the retention, the replay window and the reconciliation boundaries all follow from which it is.

ARCH_CONFLICTS.arch: FACT_TRANSACTIONS, FACT_CP_HOLDINGS and FACT_TAX_LOT, each with its own strategy — merge, merge and periodic snapshot.
ARCH_CONFLICTS.why: Holdings and tax lot are the two the design document is silent on, and a periodic snapshot is a different pattern from a merge — it is not covered by the SCD2 and merge logic that is specified.

ARCH_CONFLICTS.t: Corrections as files, or as a rule
ARCH_CONFLICTS.arch: Two correction files arrive daily and Stage 2 has a named step, correction file integration, that merges them.
ARCH_CONFLICTS.doc: Correction is a MERGE-versus-UPDATE rule applied inside the dimension build. No correction file is described.
ARCH_CONFLICTS.why: The architecture has corrections entering as data; the design document has them as a write strategy. Both may be needed, but nobody has said how a correction file reaches the rule.

ARCH_CONFLICTS.arch: A Data Quality Checks step after dbt Gold in the Airflow chain.
ARCH_CONFLICTS.doc: A per-row pass or fail computed in the STG view, before anything is loaded, plus tests between every layer.
ARCH_CONFLICTS.why: Before or after publication is the whole question. The architecture's position puts the check after Gold is written, which is where reconciliation already sits and is already a known gap.

OUTBOUND_FLOW.example: a consumer submitting through a loader file, with Pivotal CRM as the worked example

steps.t: The Orchestration Hub exposes an API. CRM calls it with the loader details and the data the loader needs.
The Hub validates what it was given and transforms it into loader format.
SEI Professional Services processes the loader.
CRM exposes an API of its own, and the Hub calls it with the response.

OUTBOUND_FLOW.note: Two APIs, one each way, and the Hub owns validation and the format. That makes the Hub responsible for a contract neither SEI design document mentions: what a valid submission looks like, what happens to an invalid one, and what the response carries when SEI rejects a loader rather than the Hub.

INBOUND_POSTURE.note: Both SEI design documents describe the file path and only the file path — a scheduled scan every five minutes, one mapped task per file, completeness measured as a set of files that arrived. If events are the primary inbound route, the completeness gate, the business-date state machine and the SLA all rest on a path that is the secondary one.
INBOUND_POSTURE.consequence: This does not make the event components a proposal any more. It makes them the primary path with no design document behind them, which is a sharper problem and a different one.

SCENARIOS.s: Exactly one pattern matches
SCENARIOS.r: One work item is created, carrying the interface, the physical filename, the business date, the target RAW table and the parsing rules.

SCENARIOS.s: No pattern matches
SCENARIOS.r: Not loaded and not moved. An unmatched-file event is emitted with the filename and path, and the approved exception-location policy applies — which is still open decision O1.

SCENARIOS.s: More than one pattern matches
SCENARIOS.r: Treated as a configuration defect. No target table is chosen, nothing is processed, and it is logged and notified.

SCENARIOS.s: The scan finds nothing
SCENARIOS.r: The run succeeds with zero mapped tasks. The completeness and SLA task still runs — which is the point, because yesterday's late file can complete the set without a new one arriving.

SCENARIOS.s: The business date will not parse
SCENARIOS.r: Rejected before any RAW write, with the parsing error recorded. The format mask must reject impossible dates even when the regex shape matches.

SCENARIOS.s: Header or trailer fails
SCENARIOS.r: RECEIVED becomes QUARANTINED, the error is recorded and the file moves to Quarantine. Nothing is written to RAW.

SCENARIOS.s: A zero-row file arrives and is not allowed
SCENARIOS.r: QUARANTINED, same path. Whether zero rows are allowed is per interface configuration.

SCENARIOS.s: The same file is discovered again
SCENARIOS.r: If the existing record is ARCHIVED it is skipped and logged as a duplicate; no second registry row is created. A unique key on the interface and business date enforces it.

SCENARIOS.s: A record is stuck in RECEIVED, VALIDATED or LOADING
SCENARIOS.r: Investigated, never reset automatically. The Airflow task state, the worker logs, the file location and the Oracle outcome are checked first, and the same record is reused for recovery.

SCENARIOS.s: The RAW load or the count check fails
SCENARIOS.r: Rolled back. LOADING becomes FAILED with the error and the end timestamp. The insert and the count reconciliation are one Oracle transaction, and the commit happens only when the file count, the trailer count and the inserted count all agree.

SCENARIOS.s: A FAILED file is rerun
SCENARIOS.r: The same registry id is reused and the retry count goes up. Any exceptional partial rows are removed through the approved process first, then the file reloads in one transaction.

SCENARIOS.s: The archive move fails after a good load
SCENARIOS.r: ARCHIVE_FAILED. RAW is kept and is never deleted or reloaded — the move happens after the commit and cannot be part of the transaction. Only the move is retried.

SCENARIOS.s: Why ARCHIVED is the ready state
SCENARIOS.r: A reconciled RAW commit is not released downstream until the physical archive succeeds, so completeness counts ARCHIVED and nothing earlier.

SCENARIOS.s: Complete before the cutoff
SCENARIOS.r: The guarded transition is taken and transformation is invoked.

SCENARIOS.s: Complete at or after the cutoff
SCENARIOS.r: Still triggered, and a recovery or late-completion event is published if the date had already breached.

SCENARIOS.s: Incomplete before the cutoff
SCENARIOS.r: The date stays PENDING, nothing is triggered, and the next scheduled run re-evaluates.

SCENARIOS.s: Incomplete at or after the cutoff
SCENARIOS.r: The date stays PENDING and a correlated breach alert is published. Correlation is event type plus business date, so a persistent breach raises one alert rather than one every five minutes.

SCENARIOS.s: The completeness query itself fails
SCENARIOS.r: The task fails and Airflow retries. Readiness is unknown, so nothing is triggered.

SCENARIOS.s: Two runs try to trigger at once
SCENARIOS.r: The second guarded update changes zero rows, so it does not trigger. The deterministic run id rejects a duplicate as well.

SCENARIOS.s: TRIGGER is set but transformation never started
SCENARIOS.r: A scheduled check retries when the status is TRIGGER, the transformation run id is null and no matching deterministic run exists.

SCENARIOS.s: A transformation task fails
SCENARIOS.r: The date stays TRIGGER, no next date is created and the pipeline is locked. Airflow alerts and the run restarts from the failed task; each layer's write is idempotent for the date.

SCENARIOS.s: FACT fails after DIM succeeded
SCENARIOS.r: The restart resumes at the fact build. The dimension is not rebuilt.

SCENARIOS.s: The restart reaches the final task
SCENARIOS.r: The date advances to COMPLETE and the next PENDING row is inserted in the same transaction, exactly once.

SCENARIOS.s: A key column is missing
SCENARIOS.r: The STG view marks the row FAIL with a reason code and INT never reads it. The row goes to the DQ store as OPEN.

SCENARIOS.s: A code is not in the mapping table
SCENARIOS.r: Same path — FAIL at STG with its own reason code, excluded before any mapping is attempted.

SCENARIOS.s: A full-snapshot entity fails
SCENARIOS.r: The row stays OPEN until a corrected record arrives in a later full file, which replays it and marks it RESOLVED. This rests on account and client being full daily snapshots.

SCENARIOS.s: A transaction fails
SCENARIOS.r: That date's records do not come round again, so it replays only on a corrected reload for the date, or when the missing dimension arrives.

SCENARIOS.s: A code has no active mapping row
SCENARIOS.r: Caught at INT as a transformation failure, owned by the transformation team rather than the source. Marked not auto-replayable: it stays OPEN until a code fix is deployed.

SCENARIOS.s: The same failure returns after a rerun
SCENARIOS.r: Expected, and the signal is that a code fix is needed rather than another rerun.

SCENARIOS.s: A transaction's dimension has not arrived
SCENARIOS.r: Never written to Gold with a placeholder key. Held in the DQ store as replayable and OPEN, re-derived from INT on a later day once the dimension exists, then marked RESOLVED.

SCENARIOS.s: A row is still OPEN at the retention edge
SCENARIOS.r: CLOSED and alerted at seven days, because the DQ store keeps lineage only and INT no longer holds the data to re-derive it.

SCENARIOS.s: A correction arrives and the row is still current
SCENARIOS.r: A normal MERGE, joined on the surrogate key rather than the natural key — a natural-key join matches both the closing and the opening row and fails.

SCENARIOS.s: A correction arrives and the interval is already closed
SCENARIOS.r: A direct UPDATE of that closed row only. Never a MERGE — it would reopen an interval that is settled.

SCENARIOS.s: Someone changes the shape of a Gold table
SCENARIOS.r: Refused. Every Gold model fails on a schema change, and the service account holds DML only — no create, alter or drop.

SCENARIOS.s: Counts do not agree at a boundary
SCENARIOS.r: The difference is written to the immutable log and published. The pass or warning verdict is derived on the Splunk side, after the data is already in Gold — so it alerts rather than blocks.

SCENARIOS.s: The held backlog is growing
SCENARIOS.r: Alerts on the ageing open rows, and the usual cause is a late dimension file.

SCENARIOS.s: DQ or reconciliation is rerun for a date
SCENARIOS.r: The DQ rows are upserted so their resolution status survives, the recon rows for that date are replaced, and both are republished.

SCENARIOS.s: Publishing to Splunk fails
SCENARIOS.r: The data is already durable in Oracle. The publish task is separate and retryable, and it is idempotent per date.

SCENARIOS.s: A successful file has to be replaced
SCENARIOS.r: Approval first, then the reason, approver, operator and affected downstream scope are recorded. The registry row and the RAW rows are deleted through the controlled process, the corrected file is dropped in Landing, and a fresh lifecycle starts. The downstream rebuild for that date is coordinated separately.

SCENARIOS.s: A quarantined file is corrected
SCENARIOS.r: The same registry id is reused, the retry count goes up, the status resets to RECEIVED and every validation runs again before any RAW write.

SCENARIO_GAPS: Invalid data types inside an otherwise well-formed file
Invalid measure values — a negative quantity, an impossible price
Duplicate rows arriving inside a single fact feed
Database constraint violations on the Gold write
Network or permission failures on the archive move specifically
Scheduler or worker restart part-way through a mapped task

RECONCILE.t: Stage 3 names two different things
RECONCILE.sup: Stage 3 IS Pre-Gold, on Oracle Exadata, and a fourth tier - Consumer Movement - carries publish and delivery with no transformation in flight.
RECONCILE.hub: The data path draws Stage 3 as the warehouse itself, with Pre-Gold as a separate layer before it and no publish tier at all.
RECONCILE.cost: Every document that says 'Stage 3' means one of two different databases. The acceptance criterion 'every component is assigned to one canonical domain and tier' cannot be evaluated until this is picked.

RECONCILE.t: DIM and FACT are in the wrong tier
RECONCILE.sup: Dimensions, facts, aggregates and control-total preparation are Stage 3 Pre-Gold, on Exadata. Stage 2 is normalised canonical entities and stops there.
RECONCILE.hub: Stage 2 INT is drawn as INT, DIM and FACT together, on the same Oracle estate - which is how both SEI design documents describe it.
RECONCILE.cost: This is not a folder move. If the supplement holds, DIM and FACT change database, the dbt chain splits across two estates, and the STG-to-INT reconciliation boundary stops being the last one that matters.
RECONCILE.where: PROC_STAGES, the stage chain, the database model

RECONCILE.t: The file lifecycle has two sets of state names
RECONCILE.sup: DISCOVERED, PROCESSING, DUPLICATE_SKIPPED, QUARANTINED, FAILED, ARCHIVE_FAILED, ARCHIVED.
RECONCILE.hub: RECEIVED, VALIDATED, LOADING, QUARANTINED, FAILED, ARCHIVE_FAILED, ARCHIVED - from the File Ingestion design document.
RECONCILE.cost: Two names for one state machine is two state machines. Operators will see one set in the registry and the other in the runbook, and DUPLICATE_SKIPPED exists in only one of them.

RECONCILE.t: Three different counts of reconciliation boundaries
RECONCILE.sup: Seven boundaries, including Stage 2 to Stage 3 and publish to consumer acknowledgement.
RECONCILE.hub: The pack specifies three. The architect review recommends twelve under an event-primary posture.
RECONCILE.cost: Nobody can say whether reconciliation is complete, because complete is three, seven or twelve depending on which document is open.

RECONCILE.t: Stage 2 retention is settled here and open there
RECONCILE.sup: Seven-day retention WHERE DEFINED, and SILVER-DEC-06 leaves retention and partition management open per entity.
RECONCILE.hub: Seven days, partition drop, stated flatly on every one of the 52 tables.
RECONCILE.cost: The replay window follows from retention. Stating it as settled when it is a per-entity decision makes every replay answer provisional without saying so.
RECONCILE.where: the INT contract, every table record

RECONCILE.t: The outbound submission registry now has a design
RECONCILE.sup: WORKFLOW_DEFINITION to WORKFLOW_INSTANCE to LOADER_DELIVERY and API_CALL, each reporting STATUS_EVENT.
RECONCILE.hub: The loader loop screen says there is no outbound equivalent of FILE_REGISTRY, so a reject count has nothing to reconcile against and a batch that never comes back never ages out.
RECONCILE.cost: Closed, if the ERD is approved. LOADER_DELIVERY plus STATUS_EVENT is the registry that was missing.
RECONCILE.where: the loader loop, the database model

RECONCILE.t: Stage 2 to Stage 3 movement has a pattern and a gate
RECONCILE.sup: Database-link or direct-path movement preserving LOAD_ID and BUSINESS_DATE, with a reconciliation gate that authorises or holds the publish scope, and a replay boundary scoped by date and load.
RECONCILE.hub: The database picture has no movement component at all - Pre-Gold simply follows DIM and FACT with nothing in between.
RECONCILE.cost: Closed in design. Still needs DEC-GAP-04 to pick the mechanism.
RECONCILE.where: the database model, the data path

RECONCILE.t: Correlation across the loader round trip
RECONCILE.sup: CORRELATION_ID propagated through Hub, orchestration, API and loader execution, callback and monitoring; IDEMPOTENCY_KEY stable across retries of the same business operation.
RECONCILE.hub: The loader screen asks for one submission id threading all four legs, and names it as missing.
RECONCILE.cost: Closed. The identifiers exist and have propagation rules.

RECONCILE.t: LOAD_ID is missing from every model we draw
RECONCILE.sup: LOAD_ID is the identifier preserved from RAW through Stage 2, Stage 3, replay and publish evidence, and acceptance criterion 4 depends on it.
RECONCILE.hub: Stage 1 adds BUSINESS_DATE, SRC_RECORD_ID, FILE_REGISTRY_ID and LOAD_TS. Stage 2's standard columns add MICRO_BATCH_ID and DBT_INVOCATION_ID. Neither carries LOAD_ID.
RECONCILE.cost: Without it there is no single identifier for one load execution across four tiers, and the Stage 2 to Stage 3 reconciliation gate has nothing to key on. This is a hole in our own model, not in theirs.

RECONCILE.t: Seven of 52 canonical models exist
RECONCILE.sup: The code sample implements Account, Account Optional Field, Asset, Reference, Tax Lot, Transaction Header and Transaction Detail. Four of those seven are mapped to fewer attributes than the canonical model defines. The other 45 are targets.
RECONCILE.hub: All 52 canonical tables are drawn alike, with no build status at all - a model and an intention look identical.
RECONCILE.cost: Anyone sizing the work from our screens sees 52 designed tables and no indication that 45 of them do not exist.

RECONCILE.t: Three foundation entities with no table anywhere
RECONCILE.sup: Workflow metadata, API configuration and a schema registry are named as control and metadata entities.
RECONCILE.hub: The database model holds five control tables. None of these three is among them, and nothing else in the corpus defines them.
RECONCILE.cost: The outbound path is configuration-driven by design and has no configuration store. Schema registry ownership is DEC-GAP-07 and unassigned.

RECONCILE.t: A consumer-oriented model is sitting in Stage 2
RECONCILE.sup: int_bbh_open_trade_star joins six INT models into a denormalised target layout and belongs in Pre-Gold or Publish.
RECONCILE.hub: Nothing. The app models the canonical layer and has no view of what is actually in the dbt project.
RECONCILE.cost: Consumer denormalisation inside Stage 2 is what stops Stage 2 being reusable: the next consumer needs a different shape and gets a second star beside the first.

RECONCILE.t: Graceful degradation has four named behaviours
RECONCILE.sup: Oracle unavailable: do not claim or advance durable state. Splunk or Integration360 unavailable: follow the buffering policy, never silently discard required evidence. SEI APIs unavailable: workflow state stays queryable, retry reuses the same correlation and idempotency keys. CP360 UI unavailable: durable state remains in Oracle and Airflow.
RECONCILE.hub: Nothing on partial failure of a dependency.
RECONCILE.cost: The third one is the sharp one: evidence silently discarded during a Splunk outage is indistinguishable afterwards from evidence that was never produced.

RECONCILE.t: Landing zone failure modes, including ambiguous match
RECONCILE.sup: Partial file exposure, duplicate physical delivery for the same logical interface and date, no configuration match, MORE THAN ONE configuration match, storage unavailable. A file matching two configurations is a configuration error and is not loaded.
RECONCILE.hub: The file screen covers validation thoroughly and says nothing about what happens before a file is matched to an interface.
RECONCILE.cost: Ambiguous match is the one with no safe default: loading against the first match silently routes a file to the wrong RAW table.

RECONCILE.t: HA and DR establish no numbers at all
RECONCILE.sup: Seven items to finalise, and the supplement states plainly that no numerical RTO or RPO is established and that values require formal BBH approval.
RECONCILE.hub: Nothing on availability, failover or recovery objectives.
RECONCILE.cost: Production readiness has a named precondition that is not started. It is honest about being unstarted, which is better than a number nobody agreed.

RECONCILE.t: The context screen credits the gateway with controls it does not yet enforce
RECONCILE.sup: GW-GAP-01: the inbound trust boundary is NOT yet demonstrated as fully enforced. GW-RISK-03: arbitrary path forwarding is a live risk until a governed allowlist exists.
RECONCILE.hub: The boundary screen lists what the single managed door buys - mTLS and OAuth to SEI, rotation in one place, retry and circuit-breaker policy, one authoritative log - in the present tense, as though all of it were in force.
RECONCILE.cost: A diagram that credits a component with controls it does not have is worse than one that omits the component: it stops anybody asking. Those claims need a 'designed, not yet enforced' state.
RECONCILE.where: the boundary screen, the gateway band

RECONCILE.t: The rate limit our design depends on is not in the operation contract
RECONCILE.sup: A governed operation declares method, path pattern, vendor target, schema version, header allowlists, timeout, retry and circuit-breaker policy. There is no quota or rate-limit field.
RECONCILE.hub: The boundary screen says rate limiting at the gateway is 'where the key-set collapser's restraint is actually enforced', and the mitigation for a consumer read-storm starving ingestion is 'separate API products with their own quota tiers'.
RECONCILE.cost: Our stated mitigation has no implementation named anywhere. The collapser proposes and nothing disposes.

RECONCILE.t: Starvation has a second cause: the gateway does not scale yet
RECONCILE.sup: HorizontalPodAutoscaler comes 'after load behaviour is validated', and PodDisruptionBudget and NetworkPolicy are listed as required but not yet in place (GW-GAP-06, GW-RISK-06).
RECONCILE.hub: The shared-quota risk assumes the gateway itself keeps up and only the SEI quota is contended.
RECONCILE.cost: A bursty set-based pull, a loader window and interactive reads share a service with no autoscaling and no disruption budget. The queue forms before the quota is reached.

RECONCILE.t: The vendor token cache is per-pod, and the storm is a named test
RECONCILE.sup: The token is cached in memory until a safe expiry boundary, and 'concurrent requests do not create a token-refresh storm' is a required test.
RECONCILE.hub: Nothing. The gateway is drawn as one band with no internal state.
RECONCILE.cost: In-memory means per-pod: every replica refreshes on its own clock, and the refresh count scales with replicas rather than with work. The puller's burst is exactly the shape that triggers it.

RECONCILE.t: The correlation identifier now has an owner and a rule
RECONCILE.sup: The gateway validates a trusted incoming correlation value or generates one, and propagates it to outbound calls, logs, metrics and traces.
RECONCILE.hub: Both the loader loop and the boundary screen ask for a correlation id minted at the gateway and carried through, and name it as not yet owned.
RECONCILE.cost: Closed. The gateway owns minting and propagation, which is the answer both screens were asking for.
RECONCILE.where: the boundary screen, the loader loop

RECONCILE.t: Rotate anything that may have been exposed - including ours
RECONCILE.sup: GW-RISK-02 requires rotation evidence and clean repository and pipeline scans for any credential that may previously have been exposed.
RECONCILE.hub: This repository carried a plaintext Oracle password in local/load-all.ps1 across more than one commit. The working tree no longer has it; the history still does, and nothing has been rotated.
RECONCILE.cost: The gateway review sets the standard and this repository does not meet it. Rotation and a history rewrite are both still open, and this has been flagged more than once.

RECONCILE.t: ARCHIVE_FAILED never reloads RAW
RECONCILE.sup: Retries the archive operation and does not reload committed RAW records.
RECONCILE.hub: The same rule, in the same words, from the File Ingestion design.

RECONCILE.t: One guarded owner of PENDING to TRIGGER
RECONCILE.sup: The missing-interface set is empty AND the atomic update affects exactly one row.
RECONCILE.hub: The same guard, drawn as the gate.

RECONCILE.t: Dimensions before facts, and no placeholder keys
RECONCILE.sup: Build dimensions before facts; late-arriving dimensions are held rather than replaced with placeholder keys.
RECONCILE.hub: The same, on the transformation chain and the Gold layer.

RECONCILE.t: An event is a notification, not the record
RECONCILE.sup: Treat the event as notification; retrieve the current record from the named SDC view by payload key; process duplicates idempotently.
RECONCILE.hub: The same, as the three event kinds and the event-then-fetch path.

S1_SHAPE.w: The DDL is per interface, declared alongside the interface rather than in a central model. FILE_SCHEMA_CONFIG.TARGET_RAW_TABLE is what routes a file to its table, which is why there is deliberately no column-mapping table: the RAW table's own DDL is the schema contract.

S1_RULES: Rows are added, never updated in place. A corrected delivery is a new row set for the same business date, not an edit.
No primary key, no foreign key, no uniqueness. Identity is asserted first in STG, and enforced first in INT.
No trimming, no casting beyond what the load needs, no code translation. The first thing that reads a row's content is the STG view.
A row that will fail DQ still lands. Rejection is a Stage 2 decision, so the evidence of what arrived survives it.
A file loads whole or not at all, and the three counts must agree before the commit.
S1_COLS: which day this row belongs to - set from the file, not from the clock
the row's identity within its delivery, so a DQ failure in Stage 2 can name the line it came from
which delivery it arrived in - the join back to the file, its counts and its archive path

S1_CONFLICT.w: The architecture names seven. The dbt design document names three - account, client and transaction. Position, tax lot and the two correction tables do not appear in it at all.
S1_CONFLICT.why: Four of the seven feeds have no transformation designed for them. If the architecture is right, the design document covers under half the inbound surface, and the gap is invisible from Stage 2 because nothing downstream asks for a table that was never modelled.

S1_NOT_HERE: No entities and no relationships - the first normalised model is Stage 2 INT.
No reference-code translation - codes land as delivered.
No deduplication - a duplicate delivery is two row sets, told apart by FILE_REGISTRY_ID.
No retention rule is stated in either document for RAW, unlike INT's seven days.

DB_CONTROL.w: What is expected: the interfaces, their patterns, their target RAW table and whether a zero-row file is allowed.
One row per interface per business date, with its counts and its lifecycle. ARCHIVED on it is what completeness counts.

DB_ABSENT.w: The event path's equivalent of FILE_REGISTRY: one row per micro-batch with a state and a count. Without it the gate cannot ask whether every micro-batch LOADED, which is half of its condition.

One row per submission threading all four legs, with counts from the status API and the id of the error-detail file. Without it a reject count has nothing to reconcile against and a batch that never comes back never ages out.

DB_NOTE: Every control table has exactly one writer. That is the property worth keeping: two writers on DATE_CONTROL is how two runs both believe they own the business date, and the guarded update exists precisely because the design refuses to rely on there being only one.

FILE_CHAIN.w: A scheduled scan of the Landing Zone, every five minutes. Repeated discovery of the same file is safe because the registry claim on (interface, business date) is what makes it idempotent, not the scan.

Each discovered file is expanded into its own mapped task, so one bad file fails one task rather than the run. The DAG itself is metadata-driven: the interfaces it expects come from configuration, not from code.

Before a single row is loaded: readable, header, trailer, zero-row policy and business date. Anything that fails here has touched no RAW table, which is what makes QUARANTINED recoverable by simply revalidating a corrected file.
The detail rows go into the configured RAW table in ONE transaction. Not one per batch of rows, not one per chunk - one per file. A half-loaded file is the state the design refuses to allow.
Parsed rows, the trailer's declared count and the rows actually inserted must all be equal. They are checked before the commit, not after, so a disagreement rolls back rather than needing a repair.
The file moves to Archive and the outcome is recorded. ARCHIVED is the only terminal success, and it is what the completeness gate counts - not RECEIVED, not LOADING.

FILE_VALIDATIONS: The file opens and parses as the configured format.
Present and matching the configured schema for the interface.
Present, and its declared row count is readable.
A zero-row file is a valid delivery, not an error - it is how an interface says it had nothing today. Treating it as a failure stalls the completeness gate on a quiet day.
The date in the file matches the date being ingested.

COUNT_RULE.w: Parsed, declared and inserted. All three are held on the registry row, so a disagreement is readable afterwards rather than only in a log. They are compared before the commit, not after it, so a disagreement rolls the transaction back - which is why a short load can never reach ARCHIVED and never counts towards completeness.

FAIL_MODES.fix: Correct the file and revalidate. The registry record is reused rather than duplicated.

FAIL_MODES.when: A technical failure, or the RAW load itself failed.
FAIL_MODES.raw: The transaction rolled back, so RAW is unchanged.
FAIL_MODES.fix: Rerun after verifying RAW state. The registry record is reused.

FAIL_MODES.when: RAW committed, then the file move failed.
FAIL_MODES.fix: Retry the move ONLY. Never reload RAW - a reload here duplicates a business date, and nothing downstream will tell you.

FILE_POSTURE.b: Under the events-primary posture the file set is described as generated and held rather than loaded. That makes the file arm of the completeness gate a recovery path rather than the daily one - and a cold standby and a running second pipeline look very different on a page and cost very different amounts to keep working.

CHANNELS.name: Change events
CHANNELS.one: SEI tells BBH that a row changed. The event carries no data.
CHANNELS.detail: Four envelope fields — eventid (a type code, not a message id), key, op (I/U/D) and view. The event names what changed and where to read it; it never carries the change itself. Published on domain topics, at-least-once, ordered within topic and partition only.
legs: SWP writes to the Snowflake intake; SDC publishes on the domain topic
Event listener consumes; markers 1000/1001 bracket each commit
Key-set collapser folds repeat keys over the micro-batch window

CHANNELS.name: Data fetch API
CHANNELS.one: BBH reads the current state of the keys the events named.
CHANNELS.detail: One bound, set-based retrieval per view per micro-batch — not per event. The same gateway and the same contract also serve an on-demand real-time read for consumers that cannot wait for the pipeline: one API, two callers.
legs: Set-based puller builds the key set for the view
Call leaves through Apigee and the API Gateway
SEI view API returns current state for the set

CHANNELS.name: File delivery
CHANNELS.one: The daily file set. Generated and held as a recovery route.
CHANNELS.detail: SWP writes to SFTP, Momentum copies complete files to the Landing Zone, discovery runs every five minutes and maps one task per file. Validate, load RAW in one transaction, three counts must agree, archive. Under the event-primary posture this is produced each day but not loaded in the ordinary course.
legs: Momentum copies complete files to the Landing Zone
Scheduled discovery, one mapped task per file, validate, load, archive

CHANNELS.name: Loader round trip
CHANNELS.one: BBH data to SEI, and the outcome back — status by API, detail by file.
CHANNELS.detail: Four legs and two transports. The status API carries the verdict and the counts; the error file carries the per-record detail. The response to the originating consumer cannot be sent until both are in and agree.
legs: Consumer calls the Hub API with loader details and data
Validate, map to SWP loader format, call the loader API out through the gateway
SEI PS processes; calls Integration 360 with status and counts
Status and error detail arrive as a file on the file transport

GATEWAY_NOTE.costs: Shared door, shared quota. The puller is bursty and must not starve; the loader has a window; interactive consumers are latency-sensitive and unbounded in number. A consumer read-storm can eat the SEI quota, ingestion stalls, and the completeness gate never fires.
GATEWAY_NOTE.fix: Separate API products with their own quota tiers per caller class, sharing the gateway but not the budget, with a reserved floor for the ingestion puller that it cannot be squeezed below.

EV_KINDS.tells: A row changed on a named SDC view.
EV_KINDS.carries: eventid, key, op (I/U/D), view. No payload.
EV_KINDS.note: The event is a notification. Nothing moves until the puller re-reads current state from the view the event names.

EV_KINDS.tells: A commit boundary on a topic — you have the whole commit, not part of one.
EV_KINDS.carries: eventId, batchDt, onlineDt. Three fields, no counts.
EV_KINDS.note: 1000 opens and 1001 closes, on every partition of every subscribed topic. The batch is consistent only when the LAST topic closes. A consumer that declares itself done at its own end marker has read part of a transaction. Ids 1000/1001 sit clear of the catalogue's 1–105 and are not catalogue events.

EV_KINDS.tells: A business process in SWP has finished.
EV_KINDS.note: Event 2 — batch date flip, EDB: end-of-day position and accrual processing has completed, and this is the gate for retrieving EOD data. Event 5 — pricing complete, price date flip. A missing system event raises the System Event SLA alert.

EV_RULES: Marker events carry no record counts, so they cannot be used for record-count completeness.
There is no required processing order between event types. If ordering matters downstream, the listener imposes it.
The stream is at-least-once. Consumers must handle duplicates; the key field is the deduplication identifier.
Events stay on the topic 7 days by default, 90 days maximum by configuration. Recovery is by moving the consumer group offset back.
Published events are immutable. An event at an offset cannot be updated, replaced, corrected or removed.
An MB Start on one domain topic guarantees the same MB Start on every other domain topic.

EV_GATE.what: One guarded UPDATE on DATE_CONTROL takes the business date from PENDING to TRIGGER. Only the run whose UPDATE changes exactly one row may invoke the transformation.

arms.name: Event arm
cond: Every micro-batch up to the boundary is LOADED
The EOD system event has been received
arms.why: The system event says SEI finished producing. It says nothing about whether BBH finished consuming. Gating on the event alone lets the transformation run on short Stage 1 — and STG to INT still reconciles, because it ties against a Stage 1 that is itself short.

arms.name: File arm
cond: Expected active DAILY interfaces in FILE_SCHEMA_CONFIG
MINUS distinct ARCHIVED interfaces in FILE_REGISTRY = empty
arms.why: Runs after every ingestion run including zero-file runs, with trigger_rule all_done. Under the event-primary posture this arm is the recovery path rather than the daily one.

EV_GATE.sla: If the cutoff passes and neither arm is satisfied: the date stays PENDING, nothing is triggered, a correlated breach alert is published. On later completion a recovery alert is published and the trigger fires. One SLA model, two triggers.
EV_GATE.nonGating: The loader error-detail file must not join the expected set. A clean outbound day produces no file; if that file is an expected daily interface, the set never empties and the inbound day never transforms. Outbound status and inbound completeness are two different clocks.

LOOP_RULES: One submission id threads all four legs, so a batch has one timeline rather than four logs.
The reject count SEI reported by API must equal the row count in the detail file. Disagreement means the picture is incomplete and the consumer is not told it is done.
SEI will resend status. The same status twice lands once.
A poller covers non-terminal submissions on a tiered cadence. When push and poll disagree, the poll wins and terminal never regresses.
The API status can say 60 rejected; only the file says which 60. So the consumer contract is acknowledge on submission, respond on completion — never request/response.
Registry row, header and trailer counts, quarantine on malformed, archive on success — the existing file framework, with the gating flag off.

LOOP_GAP.b: Inbound, FILE_REGISTRY gives every file a row and a state. Outbound, a submission has nowhere to live. Without one there is no correlation id threading the four legs, no reconciliation of the API reject count against the detail file, and no age-out for a batch that never comes back.
